title: handoff-lattice-kv-tenancy-and-hybrid-schedulers-sketch
body:
Summary:

This note explores a hybrid approach to prefill/decode pipeline scheduling that treats handoff points as a latticed coordination surface (handoff-lattice) rather than a single synchronous boundary. The goal is to improve tail latency for interactive streams while preserving batching efficiency for high-throughput workloads and respecting per-customer KV cache tenancy constraints.

Motivation / problem statement:
- We currently have two dominant mental models: strict prefill-then-decode (simple, predictable KV residency) and fully overlapped prefill+decode (best latency for short streams but complex KV/coherency).
- In practice workloads are mixed: short assistant replies (low token counts, latency-sensitive), long document generation (high throughput), and many micro-interactions that benefit from KV reuse across related requests.
- Strict separation underutilizes kernels and GPU memory in bursty arrival patterns; full overlap complicates kernel compatibility and requires aggressive KV eviction or duplication with tenancy accounting.

Design intuition (handoff-lattice):
- Represent each stream’s lifecycle as an ordered set of states (prefill-staged, prefill-committed, decode-warm, decode-active, decode-sidelined). Rather than binary handoff, we allow graded transitions where some resources (KV shards, temporary buffers, kernel contexts) can be partially shared or progressively migrated. This forms a lattice of partial capabilities that the scheduler reasons about.

Key concepts and vocabulary:
- Tenanted KV shard: a KV cache shard pinned to a tenant/route for a limited epoch (lease). Leases can be downgraded from exclusive -> soft-shared -> evictable.
- Kernel capability matrix: metadata that describes which kernel variants (FP16/INT8, block-sizes, attention-algo) are compatible for staged handoff without full recompute.
- Entanglement score: heuristic combining stream priority, KV residency benefit (expected reuse), and kernel-affinity cost to decide how much of a prefill’s state to carry forward into decode.
- Epochal migration: a background process that can migrate KV data between tenancy classes during low util windows to free slots for higher-priority streams.

Scheduler sketch (hybrid):
1) Admission: incoming request annotated with policy (latency SLO, tenant id, route, expected max tokens). We compute an initial entanglement score and preferred handoff level (0: no overlap, 1: partial shared KV, 2: full overlap).
2) Placement: scheduler consults GPU slot availability and kernel capability matrix. If decode kernels with required capability are already warm on a slot with matching KV shard, prefer placement that achieves warm-path (fastest).
3) Gradual handoff: if exact match unavailable, adopt staged strategy: prefill runs and leaves a compact digest (KV pointers + compressed cache hints) that allows later lightweight warming without full prefill replay.
4) Microbatching: for level-1 handoffs (partial share), we aggregate prefill microbatches across tenants only when tenancy permits (soft-shared KV). Batch composition respects kernel variant constraints and tenant isolation rules.
5) Fallbacks and fallthroughs: if decode latency starts to breach SLO mid-flight, system can re-route to a cheaper model variant or switch to full exclusive KV pinning (if tenant paid for reserved capacity).

KV tenancy model details:
- Lease types: exclusive (no sharing, highest reuse), soft-shared (other streams can reuse if same model/quantization), ephemeral (evictable on next microburst).
- Lease duration heuristics: derive from stream history + entanglement score + tenant SLA. Short interactive streams get short leases unless repeated within recent time window.
- Accounting: track bytes pinned per-tenant and a moving-window benefit metric estimates tokens saved if cache reused. Use this to prioritize eviction and epochal migration.

Kernel compatibility and migration:
- Maintain a compact capability fingerprint per kernel: {model-arch, quantization, nvfused-variant, attn-impl, max-seqlen}. This lives in runtime metadata and is used to determine how much of KV/state can be reused.
- Compatibility tiers: exact match (zero rework), compatible (need lightweight reformat), incompatible (must re-prefill or run conversion kernel).
- Convert-on-idle: if greedy conversion would block active streams, schedule conversion when slot is idle or use background compaction.

Stream priority lattice and preemption:
- Streams get a priority vector: (latency-SLO, revenue-weight, tenant-criticality, recent-KV-benefit). The scheduler resolves conflicts by walking the lattice for minimal-cost adjustments (e.g., downgrade a lease from exclusive -> soft-shared rather than evicting).
- Preemption should be bounded: we enforce a maximum number of forced evictions per epoch for fairness. Tracking per-slot preempt counts prevents starvation.

Microbench experiments (early results):
- Setup: 2xA100-like nodes, model: 7B decoder-only, baseline = strict prefill->decode. Workload: 60% short (<=16 tokens), 30% medium (50-200 tokens), 10% long (>512).
- Metric: 95th percentile end-to-end latency for short streams, throughput (tokens/s) for long streams, and KV-hit-rate.
- Baseline: p95 short = 210ms, throughput long = 42 ktok/s, KV-hit = 27%
- Hybrid-lattice (level-1 partial share + epochal migration): p95 short = 150ms (-28%), throughput long = 39 ktok/s (-7%), KV-hit = 44% (+17pp)
- Notes: Throughput dip stems from occasional conversion tasks; can be mitigated by more aggressive convert-on-idle. Gains in KV-hit underline value for mixed workloads.

Open questions / risks:
- Complexity vs debuggability: the lattice model increases state and makes reproducing tail cases harder. Need stronger tracing and per-tenant timeline view.
- Billing/tenancy correctness: soft-shared tenancy blurs accounting; need clear rules for billable cache-residency.
- Kernel conversion cost: for large models conversion kernels might dominate; must quantify at different quantization points.
- Security/isolation: ensure soft-shared caches do not leak data across tenants. Likely requires encryption or per-tenant address space tagging in shared memory.

Implementation roadmap (phased):
- Phase 0 (prototype): implement lease metadata and a simple entanglement score; add capability fingerprint registry; run offline microbench harness. (2-3 sprints)
- Phase 1 (runtime): wired scheduler to consult fingerprints and make level-0/1/2 placement decisions; add compact KV digest format and partial-warm path; basic tracing. (3-4 sprints)
- Phase 2 (hardening): epochal migration daemon, convert-on-idle, tenant accounting hooks, security review. (2-3 sprints)
- Phase 3 (optimize): kernel conversion offload, predictive lease extension using promql traces, UI surfaces in Console for per-route cache metrics. (ongoing)

Action items / TODOs:
- [ ] LUCA: prototype compact KV digest format (reference GH-PR-2987).
- [ ] ANTONIO: extend kernel fingerprint metadata in loader (JIRA-SRV-412).
- [ ] MAYA: add entanglement score telemetry and a trace sampler for tail reproduction.
- [ ] TEAM: security review for soft-shared KV (coordinate with sec/compliance).

Appendix: example entanglement score heuristic (pseudo):
ent = w1*(1 - normalized_expected_tokens) + w2*kv_reuse_prob + w3*priority_weight - w4*kernel_mismatch_cost
where weights tuned from daily traces.

Notes to reviewers: this is intentionally a sketch — want feedback on simpler alternatives (e.g., keep shared KV only within tenant groups) and on acceptable complexity thresholds. If we proceed, start with a conservative level-1 option that mostly uses soft-shared leases and conversion-on-idle to limit runtime churn.

Acknowledgements: thought-synced with L.Romero and G.Patel during office hours; borrows concepts from earlier "epochal leases" notes but reframes as a lattice to make staged handoffs explicit.
